extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy; those interested in method, metaphysics, and moral guidance (readers of Descartes/early modern philosophy)
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpt presenting a provisional moral code and a method for philosophical inquiry: systematic doubt leading to the cogito, rules for accepting truth (clear and distinct perception), arguments for God's existence as guarantor of truth, and three practical maxims for living while suspending final judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic doubt as methodological starting-point
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject as absolutely false all opinions in regard to which the least ground for doubt can be supposed, so as to discover what remains wholly indubitable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descartes deliberately supposes the senses, reasonings, and even waking experience might be false (e.g., dream argument) in order to clear away uncertain beliefs and find a secure foundation (leading to the cogito).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept only what is clear and distinct
rubrics_metrics.description: Accept as true nothing that does not appear more clear and certain than the demonstrations of geometry; take as a general rule that all things very clearly and distinctly conceived are true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the standard of geometric clarity and distinctness as the criterion for truth; be cautious about determining which objects are distinctly conceived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cogito as first indubitable truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The fact that one thinks is itself indubitable: 'I think, therefore I am' (Cogito ergo sum) — this is the first principle of certainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if all else is doubted (sensory illusions, dreams), the very act of doubting/thinking guarantees the thinker’s existence; use this as the foundational datum for further inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use reason, not senses or imagination, as final arbiter
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not determine truth on the basis of senses or imagination (which may deceive); rely on reason and the understanding for assurance of truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Senses and imagination can present vivid but misleading representations (e.g., chimaeras, jaundice); reason provides clearer assurance, and one should never be persuaded of the truth of anything except on evidence of reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish God’s existence to guarantee truth of clear and distinct ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Argue for the existence of a Perfect Being (God) as the source/cause of the idea of perfection and as guarantor that what we clearly and distinctly perceive is true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The principle that clearly and distinctly conceived ideas are true is ultimately secure because a perfect, veracious God exists and would not place falsity in our minds; this addresses why some ideas may be confused or false when not clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical/geometers’ style of demonstration for philosophical certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim to make philosophical demonstrations as clear and certain as the simplest demonstrations of geometry (e.g., the equality of triangle angles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical truths should be sought with the same clarity and rigor as geometric proofs; use the rules laid down to conceive ideas clearly and distinctly and proceed from those certainties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional moral code while withholding final judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: While suspending final judgment in many theoretical matters, adopt a temporary practical code of conduct (three or four maxims) so as to live comfortably and decisively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct a provisional set of maxims that allow one to act without being paralyzed by doubt; these are to be used only provisionally while inquiry continues.

rubrics_metrics.name: First provisional maxim: obey local laws and follow moderate, judicious customs
rubrics_metrics.description: In practice, obey the laws and customs of one’s country and adhere to the faith in which one was educated; regulate conduct according to the most moderate opinions generally accepted by the most judicious among those one lives with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose opinions for practice based on what is commonly and judiciously practiced rather than merely professed; prefer moderate opinions to extremes because they are more convenient and likely closer to truth if in error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe actions over words to judge others’ true opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: To ascertain the real opinions of people, pay greater attention to what they practice than what they say, because many speak inaccurately about their true beliefs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: People often do not speak exactly what they believe or may be unaware of their own beliefs — practice is a more reliable indicator of opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid promises or engagements that permanently abridge freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: Class extremes include promises that abridge freedom; avoid binding oneself irrevocably to opinions or commitments that might later prove erroneous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While some engagements (vows, contracts) are useful, one should be cautious about commitments that would prevent revision of opinion or action as one’s understanding improves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second provisional maxim: be resolute in action once a practical choice is made
rubrics_metrics.description: When acting, be as firm and resolute as possible, treating the chosen course as certain for the purposes of practice, even if the opinion is doubtful theoretically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogous to travelers lost in a forest who should choose a direction and proceed straight; when immediate action is required, choose the most probable option and act consistently to avoid paralysis and regret.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act on probability in practical matters
rubrics_metrics.description: In situations where truth cannot be determined and action cannot be delayed, choose and follow what seems most probable; afterwards treat it as certain for the purpose of practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This minimizes regret and vacillation; even absent a clear probabilistic preference, select one option and commit to it for action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third provisional maxim: master oneself rather than fortune
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim to change one’s desires rather than the world; accustom oneself to the view that only one’s thoughts are fully under one’s power, and accept external limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This discipline reduces desire for unattainable external goods, fosters contentment, and mirrors the behavior of philosophers who rise above fortune’s influence through habituation and meditation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate habitual use of the method by practice and reserved exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: Regularly exercise the prescribed method (e.g., reserve hours to apply it to mathematical difficulties and questions of other sciences) so the mind becomes habituated to clearer and more distinct conceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set aside time expressly to employ the method; repeated practice increases skill and clearer conception of objects, enabling application across different sciences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use experience (travel, observation) to test and eradicate erroneous opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: Amass a variety of experience, travel, and observe so as to root out previously accepted erroneous opinions and to supply materials for reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intercourse with mankind and diverse experience help reveal errors; practical observation and travel complement methodological reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve useful observations from demolished beliefs
rubrics_metrics.description: When dismantling old beliefs (pulling down the house), reserve the useful ruins to contribute toward erecting a new, better-founded system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Destroyed or rejected opinions can still yield observations and experiences that serve as materials in constructing more certain doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate between moral/“practical” certainty and metaphysical certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that many everyday beliefs (having a body, existence of stars) enjoy strong moral assurance but are not metaphysically indubitable; metaphysical certainty requires stricter standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even vivid sensory experiences (awake or asleep) do not guarantee metaphysical certainty; only reason and the demonstration of a guarantor (God) secure metaphysical certitude.
